data.title: VisionWave Holdings, Inc. Announces Closing of $2.0 Million Registered Direct Offering
data.description:
WEST HOLLYWOOD, Calif., Nov. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- VisionWave Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: VWAV) (the “Company”), a technology company focused on advanced defense, autonomous systems and related technologies, today announced the closing of its previously announced registered direct offering with institutional investors for the purchase and sale of approximately $2.0 million of shares of Common Stock (or pre-funded warrants in lieu thereof) together with accompanying investor warrants at a price of $0.19 per Common Unit.

The offering consisted of the sale of 10,526,313 Common Units (or Pre-Funded Units), each consisting of (i) one (1) share of Common Stock or one (1) Pre-Funded Warrant and (ii) one (1) Registered Common Warrant to purchase one (1) share of Common Stock per warrant at an exercise price of $0.57. The public offering price per Common Unit was $0.19 (or $0.18 for each Pre-Funded Unit, which is equal to the public offering price per Common Unit sold in the offering minus an exercise price of $0.01 per Pre-Funded Warrant). The Pre-Funded Warrants are immediately exercisable and may be exercised at any time until exercised in full. For each Pre-Funded Unit sold in the offering, the number of Common Units in the offering was decreased on a one-for-one basis. The initial exercise price of each Common Warrant is $0.57 per share of Common Stock or pursuant to an alternative cashless exercise option. The Common Warrants are exercisable immediately and expire 60 months after the initial issuance date.

Aggregate gross proceeds to the Company were approximately $2.0 million. The Company expects to use the net proceeds from the offering, together with its existing cash, for general corporate purposes, including partial repayment of the convertible debenture issued by the Company to YA II PN, Ltd. in the original principal amount of $10,000,000 on July 20, 2026 and working capital.

Following the closing of the offering, and after the exercise in full of the Pre-Funded Warrants issued in the offering and the issuance of 9,313,157 shares of Common Stock upon the exercise of certain Common Warrants, the Company has 41,260,663 shares of Common Stock issued and outstanding.

The Company has agreed not to issue shares of Common Stock under its standby equity purchase agreement for 30 days following the closing of the offering, and its outstanding convertible notes may not be converted during that period.

Aegis Capital Corp. acted as exclusive placement agent for the offering. Sheppard, Mullin, Richter & Hampton LLP acted as counsel to the Company. Kaufman & Canoles, P.C. acted as counsel to Aegis Capital Corp.

The registered direct offering was made pursuant to an effective shelf registration statement on Form S-3 (No. 333-297939) previously filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and declared effective by the SEC on September 1, 2026. A final prospectus supplement and accompanying prospectus describing the terms of the offering have been filed with the SEC and are available on the SEC’s website located at www.sec.gov. Electronic copies of the final prospectus supplement and the accompanying prospectus may be obtained by contacting Aegis Capital Corp., Attention: Syndicate Department, 1345 Avenue of the Americas, 27th floor, New York, NY 10105, by email at syndicate@aegiscap.com, or by telephone at +1 (212) 813-1010.

This press release shall not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy nor shall there be any sale of these securities in any state or jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or jurisdiction.

About VisionWave Holdings, Inc.

VisionWave Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: VWAV) is a technology company developing dual-use unmanned systems, autonomous capabilities, and advanced sensing solutions for defense, security, and commercial applications. Its portfolio includes the VARAN unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) platform and a suite of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and drone solutions, supported by sensing, perception, and autonomy technologies. Through technology development and strategic partnerships, VisionWave aims to deliver integrated ground and aerial systems that enhance situational awareness, support operational missions, and reduce personnel exposure to risk across military and civilian environments. For more information, visit https://www.vwav.inc.

data.title: Fulcrum Therapeutics Declares Special Cash Dividend in Connection with the Proposed Merger with Slate Medicines
data.description:
CAMBRIDGE, Mass., Nov. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Fulcrum Therapeutics, Inc. (“Fulcrum”) (Nasdaq: FULC) today announced that its Board of Directors has declared a special cash dividend (the “Pre-Closing Cash Dividend”) in connection with the previously announced merger (the “Merger”) with Slate Medicines, Inc. (“Slate”) pursuant to the Agreement and Plan of Merger, dated August 16, 2026 (the “Merger Agreement”). The Pre-Closing Cash Dividend, which Fulcrum estimates will be an aggregate of up to approximately $275.7 million, or up to an estimated $3.6095 per share, will be payable in cash to holders of record of outstanding shares of Fulcrum common stock as of December 7, 2026. The estimated cash dividend is equal in the aggregate to an amount mutually agreed in good faith by Fulcrum and Slate by reference to the amount by which Fulcrum’s Net Cash (as determined pursuant to the Merger Agreement) is expected to exceed $20,300,000 as of the closing of the Merger. The estimated per share dividend is based on 76,381,948 shares of common stock outstanding as of November 25, 2026. The total actual distribution of the amount of the Pre-Closing Cash Dividend is scheduled to be paid to Fulcrum’s transfer agent on December 10, 2026 (the “Dividend Payment Date”), and may be higher or lower than the estimated amount. The transfer agent will distribute the Pre-Closing Cash Dividend to stockholders within a few days following the Dividend Payment Date.

Payment of the Pre-Closing Cash Dividend is subject to the final determination of Fulcrum’s Net Cash in accordance with the Merger Agreement. The estimated aggregate Pre-Closing Cash Dividend amount includes approximately $7.0 million of proceeds from the sale of Fulcrum’s early-stage fetal hemoglobin (“HbF”) assets to an unaffiliated third-party pharmaceutical company, which are expected to be funded into escrow prior to the closing of the Merger and credited to Fulcrum’s Net Cash for purposes of the Merger Agreement. The closing of the early-stage HbF assets sale is contingent upon consummation of the Merger (or in the event the Merger Agreement is terminated, upon receipt of any necessary approvals). If the anticipated $7.0 million of proceeds are not funded into escrow, the Pre-Closing Cash Dividend will be reduced to an estimated aggregate of $268.7 million, or an estimated $3.5178 per share. Closing of the Merger is expected to occur on or about December 11, 2026, assuming that the transaction is approved by Fulcrum’s stockholders and the satisfaction or waiver of all conditions under the Merger Agreement. Fulcrum’s stockholders will consider and vote upon approval of the Merger at the special meeting of Fulcrum’s stockholders scheduled for 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time on December 3, 2026.

If you need assistance voting your shares or have questions regarding the special meeting of Fulcrum’s stockholders, please contact Fulcrum’s proxy solicitor, D.F. King & Co., Inc., at (800) 431-9643 (toll-free).

About Slate Medicines, Inc.

Slate Medicines is developing next-generation therapeutics designed to expand treatment options for migraine and other headache disorders. Slate’s mission is to offer migraine patients more complete freedom from their disease than is possible with the current standard of care. Slate is advancing a portfolio of potentially best-in-class therapeutics, led by SLTE-1009, a clinical stage anti-PACAP/VIP monoclonal antibody designed to enable subcutaneous, infrequent dosing. For more information, please visit www.slatemedicines.com. 

About Fulcrum Therapeutics, Inc.

Fulcrum Therapeutics is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company that focused on developing small molecules to improve the lives of patients with rare hematological disorders. Fulcrum used proprietary technology to identify drug targets that can modulate gene expression to treat the known root cause of genetically defined diseases. data.title: Canada Pumps Billions More For Battered Forest Industry
data.description:
By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--Canada unveiled on Friday a multibillion-dollar plan to reverse the dwindling fortunes of the country's forest-products sector, which is struggling under the weight of U.S. tariffs and faces acute risks unless addressed.

Canada's Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said the task at hand is to revitalize the sector and stop the flight of capital to the U.S. and elsewhere. Alongside hefty tariffs, Canadian officials acknowledged some of the forestry sector's challenges are homegrown, among them chronic underinvestment and regulatory overlap that thwarts access to cost-competitive fiber used in the production of pulp and paper.

For Hodgson's efforts, Canada has allocated an additional 6.5 billion Canadian dollars (US$4.5 billion) for forestry-sector improvements, building on C$3 billion provided in August 2025 to help with the fallout from U.S. tariffs. All told, the Canadian government has made available roughly C$33 billion in financing for all trade-exposed companies, and about C$10 billion in direct support for affected workers.

Most Canadian exports of softwood lumber - used in the construction of houses - face U.S. duties and tariffs of nearly 35%. Ottawa and Washington have engaged in a decades-long row about lumber products, with U.S. officials accusing Canada of unfairly subsidizing its forest industry.

Officials added forest-product exports have dropped 22% since President Trump imposed further duties on the sector. This has led to the closure of 12 Canadian sawmills, and output curtails in 40 other plants, the officials added.

Hodgson said the government wants to improve access to fibre, accelerate innovation in the sector, and drive domestic demand for Canadian forest products. "Business as usual is no longer an option for our forest sector," he said, adding the government's plan is meant to help the sector navigate current challenges and secure its future.

The additional money for Canada's forest sector is in response to findings from a government-appointed task force, which this year warned the industry faces an existential risk. "Continued inaction will accelerate capital flight, erode skilled workforces, destabilize rural and Indigenous communities, and forgo a generational opportunity to position Canada as a leader in the emerging global bioeconomy," the task force said.

Canada is home to nearly 10% of the world's forests, and about 40% of the country is covered by timberland. But the sector's economic heft has weakened considerably over the decades. Government data indicate that forest products account for about 1% of Canada's gross domestic product, down from a 3% level over two decades ago. Meanwhile, employment in the sector is about 40% below 2004 levels, and softwood-lumber production has declined by nearly a third from 2017 levels.

Of the C$6.5 billion made available, officials said about one-quarter of that cash will be focused on improving productivity at existing sawmills, while the remaining monies are expected to invest in new large-scale factories to accelerate the development of advanced forest products.

Write to Paul Vieira at paul.vieira@wsj.com

data.title: CUPE 5089 condemn moves by Toronto Police Services to expand in TTC and take over members’ work
data.description:
CUPE 5089 condemn moves by Toronto Police Services to expand in TTC and take over members’ work

Union argues growth of TPS presence in transit system won’t address core safety issues

Toronto Police Services representatives have indicated they intend to take over major roles in station security on the TTC, per conversations between CUPE 5089 President Denver Sanmuganthan and TPS.

“This is a serious encroachment into our members’ work and will not help keep riders safe” said Sanmuganthan. “When the police show up to our stations, our Special Constables have to direct them every step of the way. They do not know the system with any level of detail, unlike our members.”

Five stations have already been identified as initial priorities for TPS: Eglinton Station, Finch Station, Kennedy Station, Kipling Station, and Union Station. TPS will additionally add between 4 and 12 officers to Line 1 and 2. They have already indicated plans to expand significantly, partially dependent on the new municipal councillors and the recently re-elected Mayor Chow.

CUPE 5089 members are key in maintaining a safe and secure TTC system in Toronto. They are trained in public safety, health, emergency and deescalation techniques. There are no additional powers that police can exercise in the TTC. The only difference between TPS officers and Special Constables is that police are equipped with firearms and other tools.

Crucially, Special Constables are very familiar with the TTC system itself, including the layout and architecture of stations, including tunnels, blind spots, and odd corners. As frontline safety workers, they are at higher risk of assault. Indeed, assaults against workers and patrons has gone up since the pandemic, despite overall crime declining in this period by almost every measure.

TPS made similar indications that they wanted to expand into TTC stations in 2016. Upon receiving a funding increase for that initiative, TPS instead created new patrol positions outside the TTC.

When the old Transit Patrol Unit of the TPS was disbanded, TPS said the unit was “no longer required” because the TTC had “a highly capable Special Constable Program”.

Since 2016 there have been resources committed to safety on the TTC, including a 10-point action plan to prevent assaults on workers in 2022, and $4.9 million in the 2023 budget to go towards 10 new Streets to Homes outreach workers, 25 Special Constables, and a one-year pilot project with the mental health team M-DOT.

It should be noted that these reforms were not aimed to address criminal incidents. A report authored by the TTC itself states that “there is no empirical evidence that persons experiencing homelessness and individuals with complex needs are related to increased safety incidents on the TTC.”

The union argues that funding for Special Constables as well as promotion of initiatives like Streets to Homes is more effective than adding police officers to the TTC.

CUPE 5089 is circulating a Change.org petition to garner public opposition to this move by TPS and instead strengthen the Special Constables program, which you can access at this link.

data.title: Clearing out my parents' house was a legal nightmare. How can I downsize without putting my kids through the same ordeal?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

Some countercultural advice this Black Friday: stop buying stuff, plus other rules for downsizing

"Legal fees ended up eating up half the value of my parents' estate." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I have recently read and heard a lot about the recommendation for seniors to take an active role in managing their estates - specifically by downsizing, in addition to having the wills and estate plans you have advised for years. Downsizing means going through all the "stuff" accumulated over the years and weeding out the treasures and clutter we no longer use, need or want.

While many seniors do this when they move into a retirement community, plenty of us stay put in our homes for decades. My parents lived in their home from 1950 to 2020. They believed their children would enjoy going through their belongings and reminiscing after they passed, but the reality was quite different and a massive hassle.

None of us lived nearby, we argued over what to do with 70 years' worth of possessions, and eventually, lawyers and the courts got involved. Legal fees ate up half the value of my parents' estate. Downsizing is difficult because of sentimental attachments, the sheer physical energy it requires and the challenge of knowing what is valuable versus what to let go of.

In my own downsizing efforts, I've avoided the hassle of online listings, garage sales or hiring estate experts, opting instead to give things to neighbors, donate them to Goodwill or toss them. What advice can you share for seniors who have too much stuff, feel overwhelmed by the process and want to spare their families what mine went through?

Aging Downsizer

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My husband wants to sell our $1.5 million home and downsize. But this is where we raised our kids - and I can't bear to leave.

You will be surprised how quickly you forget about items once they're gone.

Dear Downsizer,

Sticky notes on furniture is no substitute for a proper will.

Your experience clearing out your parents' home is a cautionary tale. Hiring lawyers can cost a fortune and escalate disagreements that could be better resolved with a mediator. When it comes to family, going to court should be the very last resort. Aging parents can start giving away their valuable items to their children in an effort to prevent arguments later on, or put in place a system for choosing them, such as labeling items or drawing straws and allowing each child to choose an item in rotation.

Be aware that giving away expensive antiques, jewelry, or furniture during your lifetime with a combined value exceeding $19,000 per recipient in a single calendar year will require you to file a gift-tax return (IRS Form 709), even though you won't actually owe taxes unless you exceed the multi-million-dollar lifetime exemption. An important sticky note for your estate plans: Naming a third party as executor, and giving them authority in your will to sell any items your children can't agree upon within, say, 30 days, will help keep any family disputes out of court.

Without further ado - and I hope this helps you - here are some tips for clearing your house:

5 rules of downsizing

(1) Be tough. Without throwing out something valuable like an antique, a letter from a loved one or a wedding photo album that can never be replaced, you have to be ruthless when downsizing. And while the struggle is real, you need to avoid engaging in it every time you open a box. Your memories are not packed away in an attic or basement. They are in your mind and they are in your heart.

(2) Think digital. After you have had the hard conversations with your children about what they want or what they don't want, you can take photos of a treasured childhood toy before donating it or throwing it in the garbage. And a Kindle or the Apple Books app takes up less space than thousands of physical books.You can always put your favorite memories on social media or put them in a shared online folder so family members have access to them.

(3) Take it easy. The emotional labor is as challenging as the physical labor. You are, after all, sifting through your memories, which will bring up good and possibly also bad or painful moments. Take your time. You acquired these belongings over a lifetime, so why would you put yourself through the onerous task of dismantling your life in a week or a month? Commit to one big garbage bag per day. If you do two per day, take Sunday off.

(4) Out of sight, out of mind. You will be surprised how quickly you forget about items once they're gone. Anyone who has moved house and lived without their belongings for a period of time will have experienced this. Our stuff becomes part of our identity. Sure, everyone has their own treasures - a piece of artwork that won't take up too much space on a wall - but you may be surprised how quickly you forget about items once they're out of sight.

The emotional labor is often as challenging as the physical labor.

(5) Stop buying. Some countercultural advice this Black Friday - stop buying stuff that replaces the stuff you threw out. Perhaps it's that 2026 holiday sweater that looks so enticing online, even when we have a closet full of old sweaters crying out to be worn. We all love a bargain, and Black Friday and Cyber Monday tempt us to spend, spend, spend (analysts forecast spending nearing $30 billion for both "consumer holidays" this year). Don't replace the stuff you throw out.

Make spring cleaning an annual or semiannual event. As writer Evelyn Richards noted in this personal reflection in Country Living Magazine about downsizing from a three-bedroom house to a one-bedroom apartment: "Decluttering isn't just about tidying up your home; it's also about nurturing your mental well-being. When you clear out the excess and organize your space, you create a serene and stress-free environment."

It feels lighter to walk into a room where everything is in order, she writes. "This kind of order can significantly reduce anxiety and make it easier to relax. When your home is clutter-free, it's like a breath of fresh air, allowing you to focus on what truly matters. Moreover, the process of decluttering itself can be therapeutic. As you sort through items, you make decisions about what to keep and what to let go, which can be incredibly empowering."

I'm resisting buying yet another pair of sneakers this Black Friday because, like you, I have too much stuff. I sometimes wonder how much money I would have saved in my life had I stuck to a black cashmere turtleneck like Apple's late CEO Steve Jobs or a black leather jacket like Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang. You have accumulated a lifetime of memories - and, presumably, a few savvy investments in artwork and furniture - and passing those treasures on to loved ones should be a joy. Still, even the most discerning consumer ends up with clutter.

The ceramic bunny rabbit has got to go.
